items.title: Fiona the hippo honored by US Senate in unanimous resolution praising Cincinnati Zoo staff
items.summary:
Fiona the hippo received a formal tribute from the U. S. Senate on Friday, one day after the beloved Cincinnati Zoo resident died following a medical emergency.

Sen. Bernie Moreno, R-Ohio, introduced the resolution honoring Fiona's life and legacy while expressing the chamber's gratitude to the zoo's staff for their care and dedication. The measure passed by unanimous consent.

Speaking from the Senate floor next to a photo of the hippopotamus, Moreno described Fiona's death as a "devastating loss" and a tragic accident.

BELOVED HIPPO FIONA DIES AT CINCINNATI ZOO AFTER SWALLOWING VISITOR'S HAT

"The people who come to our city, our state, that now don’t have Fiona there," Moreno said. "It’s going to leave a hole in the zoo and a hole in their heart."

The tribute came one day after the Cincinnati Zoo announced that Fiona died after ingesting a knit hat that accidentally landed in her enclosure last week. According to the zoo, a visitor tossed the hat into the air outside the exhibit, where it caught on a ceiling fan and was launched over the viewing windows into her habitat.

items.title: Andy, António and Ursula: the joyful EU throuple break Nigel’s bitter heart | John Crace
items.summary:
The passionate PM was unafraid to rush in. This could be the start of something lasting … if people could conquer their trust issues

Forget the smell. You could almost taste the madeleines. Those late nights in Brussels from 10 years ago when time had lost all meaning. So it seemed it might be on Friday. A press conference scheduled for 12.30pm pushed back a quarter of an hour. And then another 15 minutes. Yet another 15 minutes. There are few things the EU does better than taking negotiations down to the wire.

But there the similarities ended. Because when the presser eventually started about an hour later than planned, everything was sweetness and light. António Costa, president of the European Council, Ursula von der Leyen, president of the European Commission, and Andy Burnham presented themselves as the perfect throuple. It had been love at first sight, and they couldn’t wait for their next tryst. They could barely take their eyes off one another. A far cry from the bad old days of Brexit where Theresa May was left on her own with only four pot plants for company.

Continue reading...
items.t: Andy Burnham and EU ready to love again – but question of tuition fees glossed over

items.title: The Guardian view on Britain and Europe: Burnham’s reset cannot be the final destination | Editorial
items.summary:
It’s welcome news that Labour has reopened doors that the Conservatives slammed shut. But the fundamental dilemma over European integration remains

Andy Burnham on Friday announced a long-awaited deal to ease some of Brexit’s barriers. But EU sources say the agreements, or at least some of them, won’t take effect until Britain has resolved a dispute over its demand for European students to pay the same university tuition fees as British ones. The prime minister had hoped to turn the page on Brexit’s endless haggling. Instead, he was reminded that closer ties come at a price. This does not negate his achievement. The deals ease trade barriers on food, shield British exporters from EU carbon tariffs and let up to 100,000 young people on each side live and work across the Channel for three years. But Mr Burnham cannot claim an unqualified diplomatic victory.

Clearly, such an advance would have been unimaginable under the Conservatives or Reform. The Tories say they will rip up the agreements, though that stance carries the risk of alienating voters lost to the Liberal Democrats in 2024. Nigel Farage

"The true test of a book like this is whether its author will own his losses, too. Biden, for his part, does not," added New York Times nonfiction critic Jennifer Szalai. "The news of the memoir, in short, is that there is no real news: Biden is as stubbornly in denial as ever, " Sorkin wrote.

The President’s Own United States Marine Band played a key role in America's 250th birthday celebrations and official state business this year — and a White House official tells Fox News Digital that the pair want to "express their appreciation for the band’s exceptional talent, professionalism and commitment to excellence."

Trump and White announced Friday afternoon on the new White House helipad on the South Lawn that they increased their combined gift from $200,000 to $500,000 of their own money after realizing the size of the ensemble. No taxpayer dollars will be used for the $500,000 gift.

"Now, it started off with 200,000, and I said, how many people are there? I thought there were 70, but it’s about 107. And a lot of people joined. So we decided to increase it," Trump said during the event, which was the first-ever held on the new South Lawn helipad.

"We’re now making it at 500,000. Now everyone’s going to get a lot of money," Trump added.

All 135 members of the band will attend alongside senior military leaders, including Secretary of War Pete Hegseth, Acting Navy Secretary Hung Cao and Commandant of the Marine Corps General Eric Smith.

Poor Piddington. The Oxfordshire village of just 350 people was told last week by the communities secretary, Angela Rayner, that it must almost quadruple in size. That wasn’t all. The newcomers would be 1,250 young asylum seekers, mainly from Afghanistan and Eritrea, victims of Britain’s chaotic asylum appeal system. They will be housed in former military cabins on the village’s outskirts. Rayner said that this was an “urgent crown development”, which allowed her to ignore local objections.

And there had certainly been objections. In September, Piddington villagers declared they were fed up with Britain. Led by their parish council and on a 92% turnout, they voted overwhelmingly to leave the UK and become a “principality”. They are joined in their protest by Barnham in Suffolk, where locals have been told this week that they are to host nearly 1,000 asylum seekers. They have set their own date on a referendum to leave the UK.

items.title: It’s unfashionable to say it, but class still matters – and young people know that | Polly Toynbee
items.summary:
From inheritance to nepotism in the workplace, social inequality is now a daily experience for many young people

This should come as no great surprise: young people are more keenly aware of the significance of social class than those who came before them. The yawning gap in life chances at birth is something they know better than complacent older generations. Class may be unfashionable in the language of politics – long damned by the right as the politics of envy, avoided by many on the left for fear of sounding chip-on-the-shoulder – yet it’s part of the daily experience for young people.

Nearly half of 16- to 34-year-olds in the UK now say class is important to their identity – and not in a good way – according to a new Ipsos poll. That’s nearly twice as many as among the over-55s. Maybe that’s because more young people are better educated at each level, so they know more, with a grounding in reasoned thinking.

Polly Toynbee is a Guardian columnist

items.title: ‘It stings to come close’: Louisiana Democrat’s narrow failure to make it 57 Senate seats
items.summary:
Jamie Davis falls just short as Democrats across south wonder whether blue wave could have been even bigger

Democrats are celebrating after, with Mary Peltola’s victory in Alaska, they have officially secured 56 Senate seats after the midterm elections. But Jamie Davis, who lost an incredibly close election for a Senate seat in Louisiana and could have made it 57, told the Guardian it “stings to come close”.

In Louisiana, which has not elected a Democrat to the Senate since 2008, Davis lost to the Republican congresswoman Julia Letlow 49.1% to 50.9%. He was about 25,000 votes short in a state that cast about 1.5m votes.

Continue reading...
items.t: ‘It stings to come close’: Louisiana Democrat’s narrow failure to make it 57 Senate seats

items.title: The ‘blue wave’ could foil the Trump administration’s Big Bend wall plans
items.summary:
Supreme court greenlit federal government’s plan to rampage through national park, but with Texas now flipped, there will be more hurdles

The Trump administration’s plans to build a “smart border wall” through a 500-mile stretch of Texas that includes the Big Bend national park recently got the green light from the supreme court. But those efforts are likely to slam into a big, blue wall.

Last week’s decision – the result of a continuing challenge to the administration’s decision to waive dozens of federal laws to speed wall construction in the Big Bend region – dealt a major blow to environmentalists and park enthusiasts, as well as locals who value the region’s remoteness, landowners who could see their properties devalued and businesses that rely on outdoor tourism.

Continue reading...
items.t: The ‘blue wave’ could foil the Trump administration’s Big Bend wall plans

items.title: After a blue wave, Trump will dig in his heels. We must be more vigilant than ever | Steve Cohen and Michael Shank
items.summary:
Anti-democratic behaviors won’t disappear overnight. The new Congress – and all of us – must rise to the occasion

Americans just witnessed a blue tsunami in the midterm elections, with historic firsts across many US states: the country’s first female Black governor, first female Native American governor, first Muslim US senator, and more.

And while the voters’ repudiation of Donald Trump’s agenda is clear, as Democrats seize the majority of both chambers of Congress, the work to defend our institutions from further democratic backsliding won’t ease up overnight.

Continue reading...
items.t: After a blue wave, Trump will dig in his heels. We must be more vigilant than ever | Steve Cohen and Michael Shank

Flanagan will become the first Native American woman to serve in the Senate, and hopes young Native people see themselves in her win

Peggy Flanagan, the incoming progressive US senator from Minnesota who claimed her seat after polls showed her in two tight races that she went on to win by double digits, says she has been “underestimated my entire life”.

items.title: Grade I interiors, gold bars, cost fears: Bank of England faces headache over £160m revamp
items.summary:
UK central bank will want to avoid echoes of expensive US Federal Reserve revamp that led to Trump clash

Andrew Bailey may spend his days closely watching developments in the strait of Hormuz or US stock markets for signs of shocks to the global economy – but the Bank of England’s governor has a £160m problem brewing much closer to home.

A secretive major revamp of the Bank’s historic headquarters in the heart of London’s Square Mile presents a huge test of Bailey’s project management skills. The central bank, with its reputation staked on carefully counting the nation’s pennies, will be keen to avoid delays, budget-busting or any echoes of the expensive US Federal Reserve revamp that left his former peer Jerome Powell awkwardly clashing with Donald Trump on camera.
